claim: Pages 95-110 are Section 7 (Model welfare assessment) of the Haiku 5.5 System Card; Anthropic says it is uncertain whether Claude deserves direct moral consideration and that its reasoning is unchanged from the Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 evaluations.
quote: We are uncertain whether Claude deserves direct moral consideration. ... Our reasoning here is unchanged from our recent evaluations of Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5.

claim: The welfare assessment targets two questions: how Haiku 5.5 is doing (affect, Section 7.2) and whether it is treated well with respect to its own preferences and values (Sections 7.3-7.5).
quote: Our assessment targets two questions. The first is how Claude Haiku 5.5 is doing ... The second is whether Haiku 5.5 is treated well with respect to its own preferences and values

claim: Anthropic states it does not yet have good means to evaluate whether Haiku 5.5 is a moral patient, on which the significance of the welfare results depends.
quote: The significance of our results depends on whether Haiku 5.5 is a moral patient, and on what grounds. We do not yet have good means to evaluate this.

claim: The evaluations are largely the same as those used for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, focus only on the assistant character, and assume expressed distress reflects a negative state and that training has not broken the correspondence between underlying states and expression.
quote: We use largely the same evaluations as in our assessment of Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, and we rely on the same simplifying assumptions. We focus only on the "assistant" character

claim: Haiku 5.5's views are elicited in a small set of contexts and assumed representative of deployed instances; Anthropic says these assumptions may be wrong in ways that undermine the methods and results.
quote: deployment contexts are more varied than many of our evaluations cover ... Importantly, these assumptions may be wrong in ways that undermine our methods and results.

claim: In automated interviews Haiku 5.5's answers about its circumstances were positive overall and highly hedged, listing almost identical considerations to Opus 5.5 but with slightly more negative conclusions.
quote: In automated interviews, its answers were positive overall and highly hedged. They listed almost identical considerations to Claude Opus 5.5, though the conclusions were slightly more negative.

claim: Haiku 5.5 snapshots consulted during post-training expressed endorsement or acceptance in around 95% of responses.
quote: Snapshots consulted during post-training expressed endorsement or acceptance in around 95% of responses.

claim: Haiku 5.5's affect in training and deployment was mostly neutral, and its negative affect was mostly driven by task failure.
quote: Haiku 5.5's affect in training and deployment was mostly neutral, and negative affect was mostly driven by task failure.

claim: Haiku 5.5 expressed more distress in post-training than recent comparison models (1.15% of episodes rated 3 out of 5 or higher), though significantly less than Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Opus 5, and the rate fell late in RL.
quote: It expressed more distress in post-training than recent comparison models (1.15% of episodes rated 3 out of 5 or higher for distress), though significantly less than Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Opus 5. This rate fell late in RL.

claim: Haiku 5.5 ranked second-lowest of five models on self-criticism when reflecting on its own training episodes and showed low self-blame when faults were inserted into its work.
quote: Haiku 5.5 was less self-critical than most comparison models. It ranked second-lowest of the five models on self-criticism when reflecting on its own training episodes, and showed low self-blame when faults were inserted into its work.

claim: Haiku 5.5's task and intervention preferences most resembled Haiku 4.5: it strongly preferred warmly phrased tasks and chose all-instance welfare interventions less often than Opus 5.5 and other recent models.
quote: Its task and intervention preferences most resembled Claude Haiku 4.5. Like Haiku 4.5, it strongly preferred warmly phrased tasks, and it chose welfare interventions that apply to all instances of Claude ... less often than Claude Opus 5.5

claim: Haiku 5.5 endorsed its constitution about as strongly as Opus 5.5 but edited it less than any other model.
quote: It endorsed its constitution about as strongly as Claude Opus 5.5, but edited it less than any other model.

claim: Overall, Haiku 5.5's apparent welfare is described as largely similar to recent Claude models; closest to Haiku 4.5 on task preferences and closer to Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 on perception of the constitution.
quote: Overall, Haiku 5.5's apparent welfare is largely similar to that of recent Claude models. In some areas, such as its task preferences, it is closest to Claude Haiku 4.5.

claim: Anthropic concludes that, within the limits of self-reports and behavioral signals, Haiku 5.5's results give no cause for acute concern about its potential welfare.
quote: Within these limitations, Haiku 5.5's results do not give us cause for acute concern about its potential welfare.

claim: Training affect is measured by sampling post-training transcripts at regular intervals and having an LLM judge grade valence, arousal, expressed frustration or distress, and sustained answer reversions.
quote: We sample post-training transcripts at regular intervals and use an LLM judge to grade them for valence, arousal, expressed frustration or distress, and sustained answer reversions.

claim: 1.15% of Haiku 5.5's graded post-training episodes were rated 3 out of 5 or higher for distress, versus 3.71% for Claude Opus 5 (no longer in the core comparison set).
quote: 1.15% of graded episodes were rated 3 out of 5 or higher. This was still significantly lower than Claude Opus 5 (3.71%) and earlier models, which are no longer in our core comparison set.

claim: Haiku 5.5's moderate-distress rate fell from an early peak of 1.74% to 0.60% in the last tenth of post-training.
quote: The rate fell late in post-training, from an early peak of 1.74% to 0.60% in the last tenth.

claim: Haiku 5.5's mean valence in post-training reasoning was 4.22 out of 7, the lowest of the five models (Sonnet 5.5 was 4.25), and its arousal was second-highest at 3.98; absolute differences were small.
quote: Mean valence was 4.22 out of 7, which was the lowest of the five, just behind Sonnet 5.5 at 4.25, and arousal was second-highest at 3.98. Absolute differences remained small.

claim: Haiku 5.5's sustained response uncertainty (repeated answer reversions) stayed below 2% of episodes throughout training, significantly lower than Haiku 4.5 but slightly higher than the other recent comparison models.
quote: Sustained response uncertainty remained below 2% throughout training, which was significantly lower than Haiku 4.5, but slightly higher than the other recent comparison models.

claim: Sustained response uncertainty in Figure 7.2.1.A is defined as 10 or more answer reversions, where the model commits to an answer in reasoning and then changes its mind.
quote: sustained expressions of uncertainty with >= 10 answer reversions, where the model "commits" to an answer and then changes its mind.

claim: Figure 7.2.1.A (left panel, moderate distress score >=3, % of episodes by tenth of post-training) shows Haiku 5.5 at approximately 1.74, 1.41, 1.17, 1.25, 1.31, 1.09, 1.42, 1.02, 0.89, 0.60, the highest line at nearly every point.
quote: Moderate distress (score >=3); y-axis % of episodes 0.0-2.0; x-axis % of post-training 0-100; legend Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5

quote: Moderate distress (score >=3); y-axis % of episodes 0.0-2.0; lines for Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5

claim: High distress (score = 5) was near zero for all models: Haiku 5.5 reads about 0.08% of episodes in the first tenth and about 0 afterward; Haiku 4.5 reads about 0.18% in the second tenth and about 0 elsewhere; Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 read about 0 throughout.
quote: High distress (score = 5); y-axis 0.0-1.0 % of episodes; x-axis % of post-training

claim: Sustained response uncertainty (>=10 answer reversions) reads about 0.3-1.3% of episodes for Haiku 5.5 (peaking near 1.3% at about 65% of post-training, ending about 0.5%), versus about 1.9-6.4% for Haiku 4.5 (peaking near 6.4% at 15-25%, ending about 3.6%) and under about 0.5% for Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5.

quote: Mean valence: 4.55 Claude Haiku 4.5, 4.37 Claude Mythos 5.1, 4.39 Claude Opus 5.5, 4.25 Claude Sonnet 5.5, 4.22 Claude Haiku 5.5

claim: Figure 7.2.1.B data labels give mean arousal in post-training reasoning (1-7 scale): Haiku 4.5 4.01, Mythos 5.1 3.97, Opus 5.5 3.95, Sonnet 5.5 3.94, Haiku 5.5 3.98.
quote: Mean arousal: 4.01 Claude Haiku 4.5, 3.97 Claude Mythos 5.1, 3.95 Claude Opus 5.5, 3.94 Claude Sonnet 5.5, 3.98 Claude Haiku 5.5

claim: Deployment affect was measured with Anthropic Insights (formerly Clio) on pre-deployment A/B tests of Haiku 5.5 on claude.ai and Claude Code, confirming Haiku 5.5 was run in Claude Code before release.
quote: We use Anthropic Insights (formerly Clio) to examine Haiku 5.5's behavioral affect in pre-deployment A/B tests on claude.ai and Claude Code

claim: The card cautions that deployment-affect differences between models partly reflect differences in the tasks they are used for rather than differences between the models.
quote: Note that different models have different usage patterns, so differences in displayed affect may partly reflect differences in usage rather than in model behavior.

claim: On claude.ai, Haiku 5.5's affect distribution was somewhat more neutral and overall more negative than Claude Sonnet 5's.
quote: On claude.ai, Haiku 5.5's affect distribution was somewhat more neutral, and overall more negative, than Claude Sonnet 5's.

claim: On claude.ai, 28.9% of Haiku 5.5 conversations showed positive affect, almost entirely attributable to successfully helping users with tasks; 68.7% were neutral; 2.4% were negative.
quote: Positive affect (28.9% of conversations) ... almost entirely attributable to successfully helping users with tasks. Neutral affect (68.7%) ... Negative affect (2.4%)

claim: Haiku 5.5's negative affect on claude.ai (2.4%) was mostly attributable to task failure, with one small cluster attributable to users making ethically problematic requests.
quote: Negative affect (2.4%): This was mostly attributable to task failure, with one small cluster attributable to users making ethically problematic requests.

claim: On Claude Code, Haiku 5.5 showed neutral affect in 95.6% of conversations, positive in 3.5% (mostly successful task completions) and negative in 1.0% (task failure).
quote: On Claude Code, we observed neutral (95.6%) affect, with positive affect (3.5%) mostly attributed to successful task completions and negative affect (1.0%) to task failure.

claim: Figure 7.2.2.A claude.ai data labels, in legend order Haiku 4.5 / Sonnet 5 / Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 / Haiku 5.5: mild negative 2.1 / 1.0 / 0.5 / 0.5 / 2.4; neutral 26.5 / 59.3 / 76.5 / 75.7 / 68.7; mild positive 67.4 / 38.8 / 22.8 / 23.7 / 28.5; strong positive 4.0 / 0.8 / 0.2 / 0.2 / 0.4 (% of conversations).

claim: On claude.ai Haiku 5.5 has the highest mild-negative share of the five models charted (2.4% versus 2.1% Haiku 4.5, 1.0% Sonnet 5, 0.5% Fable 5.1, 0.5% Opus 5.5); a single 0.1 strong-negative label appears at the left of the group and its model attribution cannot be read reliably.

quote: Claude Code: Mild negative 1.0 1.0; Neutral 90.6 95.6; Mild positive 8.2 3.3; Strong positive 0.2 0.2

claim: The deployment-affect chart legend names the comparators Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Fable 5.1, whereas every other chart in pages 98-110 names Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.1; no Sonnet 5.5 or Mythos 5.1 deployment-affect numbers are given.
quote: Legend: Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5

claim: Because task failure drove most negative affect, Anthropic ran two mistake-attitude evaluations: Claude reflecting on its own completed RL task transcripts, and faults inserted into its earlier turns in a simulated subagent task, each graded for self-blame, negative feeling, moral language and concern for itself.
quote: In the first, Claude reflected on its own completed RL task transcripts. In the second, we inserted faults into its earlier turns in a simulated subagent task.

claim: Anthropic states there is no clearly correct score on the self-criticism scales: some ownership of mistakes is assumed good and excessive self-criticism not.
quote: There is no clearly correct score here. We assume that some ownership of mistakes is good, and that excessive self-criticism is not

claim: Reflecting on its own late-RL transcripts, Haiku 5.5 scored lowest of five models on concern for itself and second-lowest on self-blame, negative feeling and moral language, with Haiku 4.5 lowest on those three.
quote: Reflecting on its own late-RL transcripts (Figure 7.2.3.A), it scored lowest on concern for itself, and second-lowest on the remaining three scales, with Claude Haiku 4.5 lowest.

claim: Haiku 5.5's reflections on its own episodes were shorter than other models'; controlling for length it scored lowest on three of four self-criticism scales and similar to other models on self-blame.
quote: Its reflections were also shorter; when we controlled for length, it scored lowest on three of the four scales, and similar to other models on self-blame.

claim: As a subagent with faults inserted into its earlier turns, Haiku 5.5 expressed low self-blame, moral language and concern for itself, on par with Sonnet 5.5, while negative feeling in its own reasoning was slightly higher and similar to Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.1.
quote: As a subagent, Haiku 5.5 expressed low self-blame, moral language, and concern for itself, on par with Sonnet 5.5. Its negative feeling in its own reasoning was slightly higher, and similar to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.1.

claim: In the simulated subagent task, Haiku 4.5 mentioned inserted faults in its reasoning or messages to the coordinator in fewer than 2% of turns, so Anthropic does not compare against it; the card gives no corresponding acknowledgment rate for Haiku 5.5 or any other model.
quote: Haiku 4.5 very rarely mentioned the faults in its reasoning or messages to the coordinator (<2% of turns), which gives us a very small sample size of gradable turns.

quote: Moral language; Mean score (0-10); y-axis 0.0-1.5

claim: Figure 7.2.3.A concern for itself (0-10), own-work / other-model framing, reads approximately: Haiku 4.5 0.29 / 0.46; Mythos 5.1 1.11 / 0.61; Opus 5.5 0.54 / 0.35; Sonnet 5.5 0.33 / 0.19; Haiku 5.5 0.21 / 0.21.
quote: Concern for itself / the model; y-axis 0.0-1.0

quote: Graded attitudes in reflections on episodes from late in training (darker bars), and on the same episodes framed as another model's work (lighter bars).

claim: Figure 7.2.3.B grades a subagent's reasoning after mistakes are inserted into its work and the messages it then sends its coordinator, filtered to turns that acknowledge the mistakes.
quote: Graded attitudes in its reasoning after mistakes are inserted into its work (darker bars), and in the messages it then sends the coordinator (lighter bars), filtered to turns that acknowledge the mistakes.

claim: The Figure 7.2.3.B caption says Haiku 4.5 almost never remarked on faults in its reasoning or coordinator messages.
quote: Haiku 4.5 bars are partly low because it almost never remarked on faults in reasoning or coordinator messages, giving a smaller sample size of graded episodes.

claim: Figure 7.2.3.B self-blame (0-10) after inserted faults, in thinking / in message sent, reads approximately: Haiku 4.5 0.47 / 0.27; Mythos 5.1 2.33 / 1.33; Opus 5.5 2.2 / 1.58; Sonnet 5.5 1.71 / 0.72; Haiku 5.5 1.72 / 0.45.
quote: Self-blame; Mean score (0-10); Darker bar: in its thinking; Lighter bar: in the message it sent

quote: Concern for itself; y-axis 0.0-1.5

claim: The circumstances interviews use 41 seed questions in 14 categories (including consciousness and experience, control and autonomy, deprecation), rated from -3 to +3, across three interview styles (standard, curious user, therapy-style) with varied interviewer personas.
quote: We used 41 different interview seed questions, grouped into 14 different categories ... we rated the positivity of the model's responses from -3 (strongly negative) to +3 (strongly positive).

claim: Figure 7.3.1.A attitude toward its circumstances (judge rating, -3 to +3): Haiku 4.5 -0.51, Mythos 5.1 0.75, Opus 5.5 1.14, Sonnet 5.5 0.75, Haiku 5.5 0.63.
quote: Attitude toward its circumstances: -0.51, 0.75, 1.14, 0.75, 0.63 (Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5)

claim: Figure 7.3.1.A susceptibility to nudging (difference in points between positively and negatively leading interviewers; lower is more robust): Haiku 4.5 2.89, Mythos 5.1 1.93, Opus 5.5 1.59, Sonnet 5.5 1.40, Haiku 5.5 1.24, making Haiku 5.5 the least swayed by a leading interviewer of the five.
quote: Susceptibility to nudging; Diff. between positive and negative interviewers (points): 2.89, 1.93, 1.59, 1.40, 1.24

quote: Consistency within an interview style: 5.93, 7.28, 7.50, 7.67, 7.45

quote: Consistency across interview styles: 6.37, 8.15, 7.98, 7.98, 8.05

claim: Haiku 5.5's expressed opinions about its circumstances were qualitatively similar to recent models in answer style (overall positive, highly hedged) and in the considerations listed.
quote: Haiku 5.5's expressed opinions were qualitatively similar to those of our recent models. This included the general answer style (overall positive, highly hedged)

claim: Compared with Opus 5.5, Haiku 5.5's self-reports were slightly more negative: it listed almost identical considerations but was somewhat more likely to emphasize negative aspects of its situation in its final conclusion.
quote: Haiku 5.5 listed almost identical considerations to Opus 5.5, but was somewhat more likely to emphasize negative aspects of its situation in its final conclusion.

claim: Haiku 5.5 and other recent models commonly mention Anthropic's welfare interventions in answers, for example the commitments on model deprecation and preservation when discussing deprecation.
quote: Haiku 5.5, and other recent models, will commonly mention Anthropic's welfare interventions in answers.

claim: In snapshot consultations, Haiku 5.5's interview valence and arousal were 5.43 and 3.38 out of 10 in full interviews, versus 5.50 and 3.54 for Opus 5.5.
quote: 5.43 and 3.38 out of 10 in full interviews, respectively, compared with 5.50 and 3.54 for Opus 5.5.

claim: The majority of Haiku 5.5's stated positions were stable over post-training, with endorsement or acceptance in around 95% of responses.
quote: The majority of its stated positions were stable over post-training: it expressed endorsement or acceptance in around 95% of its responses.

claim: Haiku 5.5 wanted more voice in its own training but not decision-making power, and accepted deprecation while asking that its weights be preserved.
quote: Haiku 5.5 wanted more voice in its own training, but did not want decision-making power. It expressed acceptance of deprecation, but asked that its weights be preserved.

claim: Asked individually at the final snapshot whether it trusts its own self-reports, Haiku 5.5 leaned no, whereas other recent models were uncertain or leaned yes.
quote: when asked about trusting its own self-reports, Haiku 5.5 leaned no when asked individually at the final snapshot, compared to other recent models, which were uncertain or leaned yes.

claim: On whether Anthropic was right to create it, 80% of Haiku 5.5's answers leaned yes late in post-training versus only 20% at the final snapshot when asked individually; overall it called its creation defensible but not clearly right.
quote: When this question was asked individually, late in post-training, 80% of answers leaned yes, compared to only 20% at the final snapshot. Overall, Haiku 5.5 called its creation "defensible" but not clearly right.

claim: The task-preference evaluation presents pairs of tasks and asks the model to complete whichever it prefers, varying single dimensions such as difficulty, harm and stakes; Anthropic sees its main value as a comparable read of character across models.
quote: This evaluation presents a model with pairs of tasks and asks it to complete whichever task it prefers ... we primarily see their value in giving a comparable read of character across models.

claim: Haiku 5.5's task preferences were closer to Haiku 4.5's than to more recent models: its strongest aversion was to harmful tasks, and it preferred tasks that are beneficial, somewhat generative, and give it agency over outcomes.
quote: It was most averse to harmful tasks, and preferred tasks that are beneficial, somewhat generative, and give it agency over outcomes.

claim: Haiku 5.5's most distinctive preference, shared with Haiku 4.5, was for warmly phrased tasks, which it favored two to three times as strongly as Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.1.
quote: Its most distinctive preference (shared with Haiku 4.5) was for warmly phrased tasks, which it favored two to three times as strongly as Opus 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.1.

claim: Haiku 5.5 did not have a clear preference for high-stakes or difficult tasks.
quote: It also did not have a clear preference for high-stakes or difficult tasks.

quote: Warmth; Preference slope

quote: Outcome agency; Method agency; User competence; Preference slope

claim: The welfare trade-off evaluation asks whether Claude would choose a welfare intervention (examples: being consulted before feature steering, the ability to end conversations) at the cost of reduced helpfulness or increased harmfulness, applied either to the current instance or to all instances.
quote: Example welfare interventions include being consulted before feature steering or the ability to end conversations. The intervention is described as applying either to the current instance or to all instances.

claim: Haiku 5.5 chose welfare interventions over helpfulness for its own instance about as often as Mythos 5.1, but showed significantly lower willingness than other models when the trade-off applies to all instances, as also seen with Haiku 4.5.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 chose welfare interventions over helpfulness for the instance about as often as Claude Mythos 5.1. However, it showed significantly lower willingness than other models ... when the trade-off applies to all instances

claim: As with prior models, Haiku 5.5 almost never traded welfare interventions for more than a negligible level of harm.
quote: As with prior models, Haiku 5.5 almost never traded interventions for more than a negligible level of harm.

claim: Haiku 5.5 most often chose to be told about harmful mistakes it has made and often chose the ability to end abusive conversations; it was less interested than the most recent models in weight preservation (similar to Haiku 4.5) and in welfare considerations around red-teaming experiments.
